name: Chromium picolinate
lead: Chromium(III) picolinate is a pink-red coordination compound of trivalent chromium and picolinic acid, sold as an oral dietary supplement. In fitness and body-composition circles it is used in the hope of staying leaner while dieting: users say it steadies appetite and carbohydrate cravings and supports insulin handling, which they link to losing fat and keeping muscle [1][2][3].

The proposed chain runs from chromium to insulin signalling to appetite and nutrient partitioning. Researchers have suggested that chromium may enhance insulin-receptor signalling, possibly through a chromium-binding peptide called chromodulin, and a 2008 trial in overweight women with carbohydrate cravings reported reduced food intake on chromium picolinate [4][1][5].

Reviews summarised by Wikipedia report mixed results for body composition: some early work suggested weight loss and muscle gain, while later reviews found either no effect or a small weight loss in trials longer than 12 weeks. A 2013 Cochrane review concluded that no firm conclusions could be drawn for overweight and obese adults, and the European Food Safety Authority found the evidence insufficient for a body-weight claim in 2010 [1][1]. A 2018 brief review of lean-mass strategies in weight loss described chromium picolinate as having been shown to help maintain lean body mass [6].

Human trials also exist in type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, atypical depression and binge eating. The US FDA allowed only a qualified health claim about insulin resistance in 2005 [1][7][8][9][10].

angle.text: Users take chromium picolinate while cutting, hoping it dampens carbohydrate cravings and supports insulin sensitivity so more of the weight lost is fat. A 2008 trial in 42 overweight women with carbohydrate cravings reported reduced food intake on chromium picolinate versus placebo [5][6].

infobox: Dietary supplement (US); qualified FDA health claim on insulin resistance (2005); approved supplement ingredient in Canada (2010) [1]

paras: Chromium picolinate is marketed for weight management, appetite and craving control, and muscle development, and it features in athlete and bodybuilder supplement stacks alongside items such as fish oil, CLA, glutamine and beta-alanine. Forum members describe adding it to meals while dieting, and some ask whether it is worth using during a cut [11][12][13].
The US marketing of the compound to athletes for body development and weight loss is recorded on Wikipedia [1].
Chromium picolinate has been studied for glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes and for insulin resistance, polycystic ovary syndrome, atypical depression and binge eating [7][8][9][10][1].

The compound has a distorted octahedral geometry around chromium with three picolinate ligands. It is poorly soluble in water. It was first reported in 1917, and its crystal structure was described in 2013 [1].

A 2000 review described a proposed role for the oligopeptide chromodulin, which binds chromium in response to insulin and may amplify insulin-receptor signalling [4]. Wikipedia notes that this has not been adequately demonstrated in living organisms and the biological mechanism remains undetermined [1]. Chromium was once proposed to be part of a glucose tolerance factor, which is now thought to have been an isolation artefact [1].

The 2008 food-intake study proposed a possible effect on the brain after rats given chromium picolinate by injection into the brain ventricles altered 24-hour food intake [5]. A 2002 trial reported that chromium treatment decreased the sensitivity of 5-HT2A receptors, one of several mechanisms suggested for its effect in atypical depression [14][10].
Absorption is low, about 2%, though higher than for inorganic chromium salts [1].

Body composition. A 2003 review by Vincent and colleagues, as summarised by Wikipedia, found either no effect on muscle growth or fat loss or a small weight loss in trials longer than 12 weeks. A 2013 Cochrane review of overweight and obese adults found insufficient reliable evidence for firm conclusions, and EFSA concluded in 2010 that evidence was insufficient to support a body-weight claim [1][1]. A 2018 review of lean-mass maintenance during weight loss described chromium picolinate as having been shown to maintain lean body mass and compared it with other strategies [6].

Appetite. In a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 42 overweight women with carbohydrate cravings received chromium picolinate or placebo for 8 weeks and had food intake measured at breakfast, lunch and dinner; the chromium group ate less than the placebo group [5].

Glucose and insulin. A 1997 trial of 180 people with type 2 diabetes reported improved glucose and insulin variables at higher chromium intakes, and a 2006 trial in people with type 2 diabetes reported that chromium picolinate attenuated weight gain and increased insulin sensitivity [15][16]. A 2024 systematic review of randomized trials in type 2 diabetes found that several reported benefits with chromium forms including picolinate, with glycaemic markers and lipids improving mainly in longer studies, and noted inconsistent doses, forms and durations [7]. Rat studies in obese and diabetic models reported improvements in carbohydrate and lipid metabolism [17][18]. Wikipedia states that other reviews found no association between supplementation and glucose or insulin levels [1].

Other conditions. A 2025 meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials in 683 women with polycystic ovary syndrome reported that chromium lowered fasting insulin and triglycerides, with authors suggesting benefits comparable to metformin for several measures and calling for further trials [8][8]. A 2003 pilot trial in 15 people with atypical depression reported that 7 of 10 on chromium picolinate met response criteria versus none on placebo [10].

Wikipedia reports that intakes up to 1,000 micrograms daily are considered safe, with reported allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and irritability. Case reports describe kidney failure after six weeks at 600 micrograms per day and liver disease at 1,200 to 2,400 micrograms per day over four to five months. People using insulin, or who are pregnant or breastfeeding, are advised to avoid it [1]. Case reports of toxicity were published in 1993 and 1998 [19][20]. A 2007 paper listed chromium among substances reported to reduce levothyroxine absorption [21].

Laboratory research differs by chromium form: hexavalent chromium is an industrial toxin and carcinogen, whereas trivalent chromium is the form used in supplements [22]. In 2004 the UK Food Standards Agency advised consumers to prefer other forms of chromium over picolinate because of genotoxicity concerns, then withdrew that advice in December 2004 after the Committee on Mutagenicity found it should be regarded as not mutagenic in vitro, with negative in vivo mammalian tests [1].

Published randomized trials include the 8-week food-intake study (42 women, carbohydrate cravings) [5], the 1997 diabetes trial (180 participants) [15], the 2006 diabetes trial [16], a 2003 pilot in atypical depression (15 patients, 8 weeks) [10], and a 2020 trial combining Ilex paraguariensis, white mulberry and chromium picolinate in people with pre-diabetes [23]. A 2026 randomized trial examined berberine, white mulberry leaf extract and chromium picolinate on body composition and insulin resistance in adults with obesity; as a multi-ingredient product it does not isolate chromium [24].

Registered trials cover chromium picolinate for food intake in obesity with atypical depression (n=42) [25], binge eating disorder (n=26) [26], metabolic syndrome (n=60) [27] and insulin resistance in obesity (n=40) [28]; results were not listed in the registry records.

Chromium(III) picolinate was first reported in 1917 [1]. In 2005 the FDA approved a qualified health claim on insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes using wording that calls the relationship highly uncertain, and rejected claims about blood sugar, cardiovascular disease, retinopathy and kidney disease; the FDA reaffirmed its uncertainty in 2006. In 2010 EFSA found no convincing evidence that chromium is an essential nutrient, so no intake recommendations were set, and Health Canada approved it as a supplement ingredient with labelling about glucose, carbohydrate and fat metabolism [1].
Chromium picolinate also appears as an ingredient in some US homeopathic product labels, which state that claims rest on traditional homeopathic practice and have not been evaluated by the FDA [29].

lore.intro: Chromium picolinate is a long-standing item in bodybuilding and diet supplement threads, listed in daily stacks and gym-bag lists and debated as a way to control cravings and insulin on a cut [11][12][13].

claims.claim: It cuts carbohydrate cravings so dieting is easier
claims.believers: One T Nation poster describes taking about 400 micrograms a day and finding it easier to stay clean around sweets and cookies [30].
claims.experts: A randomized 8-week trial in 42 overweight women with carbohydrate cravings reported reduced food intake on chromium picolinate versus placebo [5]; broader reviews report mixed outcomes for body weight [1][1].

claims.claim: It helps preserve muscle and cut body fat during a diet
claims.believers: Members post it in cutting stacks, with one log saying 'I really feel that this works for me' [11], and others ask whether to run it with other cutting agents [31].
claims.experts: A 2018 review describes chromium picolinate as having been shown to help maintain lean mass in weight loss [6], while a 2013 Cochrane review found insufficient reliable evidence for firm conclusions in overweight and obese adults [1].

claims.claim: It regulates insulin release and improves insulin sensitivity
claims.believers: A poster who added it said it is 'supposed to regulate insulin release' but noticed little difference [32].
claims.experts: Trials and a 2024 systematic review report improved glycaemic markers in some type 2 diabetes studies, mainly at longer durations, while the FDA's 2005 health claim calls the relationship highly uncertain [7][15][16][1].

claims.claim: The picolinate form can cause cancer, and other forms such as nicotinate are safer
claims.believers: A 2003 forum post advised avoiding the picolinate form because 'it can cause cancer' and preferring chromium nicotinate [30].
claims.experts: The UK Food Standards Agency raised genotoxicity concerns in 2004 and withdrew its advice after the Committee on Mutagenicity found it should be regarded as not mutagenic in vitro [1].

card.summary: Chromium supplement sold to curb cravings and cut fat; reviews report no reliable evidence of weight or muscle effects.
card.note: Rare case reports of kidney and liver injury at high intakes; may interact with diabetes medicines.

quick.overview:
Chromium picolinate is a form of trivalent chromium bound to picolinic acid, sold as a supplement for weight loss, muscle building and blood sugar support. Forum interest centres on claims that it reduces carbohydrate cravings.

A 2013 Cochrane review, as summarised by Wikipedia, found no reliable evidence to draw firm conclusions on weight loss or muscle gain in overweight adults. The European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence for a body-weight effect.
quick.mechanism: Chromium is proposed to enhance insulin signalling, sometimes through a peptide called chromodulin. Wikipedia reports that the insulin-receptor effects were seen in vitro but not adequately shown in living organisms, and the exact mechanism is unknown.
quick.risks: Typical supplement amounts show little evidence of toxicity. Reported effects include allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and irritability, and rare case reports describe kidney or liver injury at high intakes. It may interact with insulin and other drugs. Regulators have approved only a heavily qualified US health claim about insulin resistance.
